reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice / Low's Clinical Autonomic Disorders
clinicalPearls: A life-threatening emergency occurring in patients with spinal-cord injury at or above the sixth thoracic (T6) level
Triggered by a noxious stimulus below the level of the lesion, most often bladder distension from a blocked catheter or bowel impaction
Presents with severe paroxysmal hypertension, a pounding headache, and flushing and sweating above the lesion, with pallor, piloerection, and cool skin below it
Reflex bradycardia and nasal congestion are common, and blurred vision and anxiety may occur
Uncontrolled hypertension can cause seizures, intracranial haemorrhage, retinal detachment, or death
Immediate management: sit the patient upright, loosen tight clothing, and urgently identify and remove the triggering stimulus (relieve the bladder or bowel)
If severe hypertension persists after the trigger is removed, rapid-onset, short-acting antihypertensive agents are used
Patient and carer education on prevention and early recognition is essential, as episodes commonly recur
reference.pathophysiology: Autonomic dysreflexia arises when a spinal-cord lesion at or above the sixth thoracic segment disconnects the splanchnic sympathetic outflow from supraspinal inhibitory control. A noxious stimulus below the injury, such as a full bladder, generates afferent impulses that trigger an unmodulated reflex sympathetic discharge below the lesion, producing widespread vasoconstriction and a steep rise in blood pressure. Baroreceptors detect the hypertension and drive compensatory parasympathetic (vagal) outflow, causing bradycardia together with vasodilatation, flushing, and sweating above the level of the lesion. However, descending inhibitory signals cannot cross the injury to switch off the sympathetic storm below it, so the hypertension persists until the offending stimulus is removed.
additionalInvestigations: Immediate and serial blood-pressure and heart-rate monitoring, referenced to the patient's usually low baseline
Bladder assessment for catheter patency and urinary retention with a bladder scan
Cautious rectal examination for faecal impaction using topical anaesthetic
Urinalysis and culture to identify urinary tract infection as a trigger
Skin survey for pressure injury, ingrown toenail, or other cutaneous triggers
ECG and, when neurological features are present, brain imaging to exclude intracranial haemorrhage
redFlags: Blood pressure rising markedly above the patient's baseline
Severe headache with neurological signs suggesting intracranial haemorrhage
Hypertension persisting despite removal of the presumed trigger
reference.prognosis: With prompt recognition and removal of the trigger an episode usually resolves quickly, but delayed treatment of the hypertensive surge can cause stroke, seizures, or death; recurrent episodes are common in susceptible patients and warrant preventive strategies.
pitfalls: Laying the patient flat, which raises blood pressure further, instead of sitting them upright
Failing to look for and relieve a blocked catheter or bowel impaction as the first step
Missing the diagnosis in a patient whose baseline blood pressure is low, so a 'normal' reading is actually a dangerous surge
Treating the hypertension pharmacologically without removing the underlying noxious stimulus
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: First-line rescue is postural: sit the patient fully upright and loosen any constrictive clothing or abdominal binder to blunt the hypertensive surge
Urgently seek and remove the noxious trigger, relieving bladder distension by unblocking, flushing or replacing the catheter and clearing faecal impaction after applying topical local anaesthetic

If severe hypertension persists once obvious triggers are excluded, give a rapid-onset short-acting antihypertensive such as sublingual glyceryl trinitrate or nifedipine, titrated to the patient's low baseline
Monitor blood pressure and heart rate continuously against the individual's habitually low baseline until the episode fully settles
Search for and treat less obvious cutaneous or visceral triggers, including pressure injury, ingrown toenail, tight garments and occult infection
Prevent recurrence through structured bladder and bowel regimens, meticulous catheter and skin care, and education of the patient and carers with an emergency alert card
Escalate to emergency care and the spinal-injury team if hypertension is refractory or complicated by seizures, visual loss or suspected intracranial haemorrhage
